core_claim.quote: In other words, both Stage 1 and Stage 2 processing are unconscious, no matter what areas are reached.

source.citation: Lamme VAF. How neuroscience will change our view on consciousness. Cognitive Neuroscience 1(3):204-220, 2010 (discussion paper; commentaries and response follow on pp. 220-240)

prediction.statement: A stimulus whose processing is cut off before recurrent processing can start (for example by a strong mask shown right after it) is not seen, even though its signals still reach high-level and prefrontal areas and can still affect behaviour.

first_stated.passage: Many studies, in both humans and monkeys, indicate that no matter what area of the brain is reached by the feedforward sweep, this in itself is not producing (reportable) conscious experience.

source.citation: Lamme VAF. Towards a true neural stance on consciousness. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 10(11):494-501, 2006

prediction.test_for: A masked stimulus that people cannot detect above chance still evokes activity in high-level visual or prefrontal areas, or still changes behaviour (for example slows a response), while the late recurrent signals in visual cortex are absent.
prediction.test_against: A stimulus whose processing has been restricted to the first forward pass (recurrent signals in visual cortex shown to be absent) is nonetheless detected and reported as seen.

other_statements_of_the_prediction.passage: A neural argument against the former would be that activation of cortical neurons per se, even activation of frontoparietal neurons, is insufficient for conscious experience, as is shown by various masking experiments

source.citation: Lamme VAF. Towards a true neural stance on consciousness. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 10(11):494-501, 2006

other_statements_of_the_prediction.passage: Apparently, a feedforward convergence of information towards the prefrontal cortex in itself is not yielding any conscious sensation, even when this information activates processes such as control and inhibition.

source.citation: Lamme VAF. How neuroscience will change our view on consciousness. Cognitive Neuroscience 1(3):204-220, 2010 (discussion paper; commentaries and response follow on pp. 220-240)
